title: Antimalware Scan Interface
summary: The Antimalware Scan Interface is a Windows interface that lets applications and scripting runtimes hand content to the installed antimalware provider for inspection before that content is executed, interpreted or loaded. Its importance comes from the gap it fills: script engines and dynamic runtimes do not necessarily write a file to disk before running code, so a traditional file scanner sees nothing to inspect. By calling into AMSI, a participating host such as a scripting engine, an office macro runtime, or a dynamic scripting component can submit the script text, the decoded buffer or the module being loaded, and the antimalware provider can return a verdict that causes the host to abort. AMSI is not itself a detection engine; it is a broker, and its effectiveness depends entirely on the provider behind it and on the host actually calling it with useful content. That dependency is the source of its well-known weaknesses. Bypass research concentrates on preventing the scan rather than defeating the signatures: corrupting the in-memory state of the interface so that calls fail open, patching the provider's scanning function inside a process, or structuring code so that the meaningful payload never appears in a single buffer that gets submitted. Because several of these approaches leave distinctive artefacts, AMSI remains valuable to defenders: failures of the interface, unexpected patching of its components, and mismatches between what a script claims to do and what the provider observed are all high-signal events when the relevant logging is enabled, and AMSI output frequently feeds straight into endpoint detection platforms.
objectives: Explain what AMSI is, how a participating host submits content, and why the design closes a scripting visibility gap.
Identify which runtimes and applications call AMSI and what each contributes to endpoint detection.
Describe the classes of AMSI bypass at a conceptual level and the artefacts each tends to leave behind.
Detect tampering with AMSI components by monitoring module integrity and provider load failures.
Assess the limitations of AMSI against encoded, segmented or encrypted content that never reaches it intact.
Integrate AMSI verdicts and errors into endpoint alert triage alongside script block and process telemetry.

beginner.definition: AMSI stands for Antimalware Scan Interface. It is a Windows feature that lets programs hand over the content they are about to run to your antivirus tool for a quick check. If the check fails, the program stops instead of running the code.
beginner.whyItMatters: Scripts and macros often run without ever being saved as a normal file. A classic file scanner has nothing to look at, so the bad code slips past. AMSI closes that gap by asking the antivirus to inspect text and memory just before it runs. It is not a scanner itself. It is a messenger, so it only works when the app calls it and the antivirus answers.
howItWorks: A program that runs scripts, such as a command shell, prepares some code to run.
Before running it, the program sends the text or memory content to AMSI.
AMSI passes that content to the antivirus product installed on the machine.
The antivirus checks the content and sends back a verdict of clean or harmful.
If the verdict says harmful, the program cancels the action instead of running it.
Because the scan happens in memory, no file needs to exist on the disk.
beginner.example: Picture an airport security queue. Before you reach the gate, an officer looks inside your bag. The gate itself does not check anything. It only opens for people who passed the earlier check. The scanning interface plays that officer for scripts. When a script is about to run, the program asks the security software to look at it first. If the officer says stop, the script never reaches the gate. If the app never asks, nothing gets checked at all.
takeaways: AMSI is a messenger, not a scanner; the antivirus behind it does the real work.
It exists because scripts can run in memory without leaving a file behind.
Watch for apps that fail to call AMSI, because that gap can hide harmful code.
